To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
aging is associated, on average, with a 20% decline in maintenance energy requirement in dogs, and a constant energy requirement in cats.

aging is associated in all species with a decrease in maintenance energy requirements, which is equivalent to 20% of adult maintenance energy requirements, and that this decrease is caused by a decrease in both basal metabolic rate and physical activity.

aging is associated, in humans and dogs, with a gradual decline (approximately 20%) in maintenance energy requirement, whereas in cats, there is little or no decline in maintenance energy requirement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of aging on energy intake and requirements in dogs and cats, with a view to developing recommendations for the feeding of senior pets.
the effects of aging on the energy requirement of dogs and cats.
the effects of aging on maintenance energy requirements in companion animals and humans, and the implications of this for feeding regimens for companion animals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aging is associated in all species with a decrease in physical activity and a decline in basal metabolism, but the relative contributions of these two factors are not known.
the maintenance energy requirement for adult cats is the same as that of young adult cats and that the requirement for adult dogs is approximately 20% less than that of young adult dogs.
aging is associated in all species with a gradual decline of maintenance energy requirements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the maintenance requirements of senior dogs and cats are lower than those of young adults, but that the magnitude of the decrease is less than previously thought.
the maintenance energy requirements of dogs decrease with age and that of cats does not.
, for dogs and cats, the maintenance energy requirement declines as the animal ages.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is inappropriate to assume that the energy requirements of senior dogs and cats are the same as for young adults.
it is not appropriate to decrease energy intake by 20% for all aging animals.
the energy requirement for senior cats and senior dogs is different from that for younger adults of the same species, and this should be taken into consideration when developing feeding regimens.
